text: A policy is just JSON, and AWS reads it completely literally — no implied intent, only the Effect, Action, and Resource actually written on the page.

Effect is Allow or Deny, nothing else. Action is the specific API call, written as service colon action name. Resource is the ARN it applies to — and notice this S3 example needs two ARNs, the bucket itself for ListBucket and a slash-star wildcard for GetObject on the objects inside it.

Policies attach two ways: identity-based, attached to a user, group, or role, answering 'what can this identity do.' Resource-based, attached to the resource itself — like an S3 bucket policy — which is the only type that names a Principal. And across all of it, an explicit Deny anywhere always wins over any Allow.

You'll also choose between managed and inline policies. AWS managed policies are broad and convenient. Customer managed policies — ones you write and version yourself — are the production standard for pipeline roles. Inline policies are for one-off exceptions tied to a single identity.
That's the full anatomy of what decides access. Next up: putting it to work — scoping a real data pipeline's permissions down to exactly what it needs, and nothing more.
